3. In 2023 readers read "novel" as new to science; the correction says it meant new to the prediction platform, not necessarily new to science, drops the word from the title, and reports 36 compounds confirmed by manual re-analysis. The paper was corrected, not retracted.
5. Not for: claiming a material is new to science; publishing identifications no expert has re-checked; disordered products the analysis cannot separate. Limits: automated XRD analysis can misidentify phases; manual analysis only when the automated fit was poor; 4 of 40 results inconclusive from XRD alone.

### Check Yourself {.unnumbered}
**19.1** (1) What counts as correct and who confirms it; protected data; written rules; who bears an error (§19.1). (2) Health coursework includes placement work whose words can reach a patient, so the field's rules raise the floor to an approval gate; in business, a check point by the writer suffices (§19.1).
**19.2** (1) The source or person a field accepts as able to confirm a result, e.g., the datasheet or standard in engineering, the archive record in history (§19.2). (2) In this book's reading: trained people are epigraphy's verification authority, and the model's first suggestion was still wrong in about 38% of restorations; experts choose among ranked suggestions (§19.2).
**19.3** (1) The §12.5 table is a starting floor; a field rule (placement policy, IRB protocol, consent form, HIPAA's de-identification standard, an employer's policy) can still say no (§19.3). (2) Any two: health information (HIPAA); education records (FERPA); research-participant data (informed consent, IRB); client files (contracts, professional duties) (§19.3).
**19.4** (1) Syllabus and instructor, program, placement or employer, professional code and licensing board, journals and funders, law; start nearest because those rules are the most specific to your work, you can ask their writers, and they are often the strictest (§19.4). (2) Who checks, who discloses, and what data may go in (§19.4).
**19.5** (1) It is the smallest working version, built to be run, checked and changed, and tested on three inputs; it claims nothing beyond them (§19.5). (2) The design (step map, action table, people points); A11 already graded them, so they earn points only if revised for the build and a run or the peer test shows them working on it (§19.5, A13 brief).
**19.6** (1) They read your words as a non-specialist and do not share your blind spots about what the outputs should mean (§19.6). (2) When it describes or affects people; with three runs each, any gap is a lead, worth a bigger test, not a conclusion (§19.6).
**19.7** (1) A short document published with a model that states what it is for and not for, how it was evaluated, including results by group where relevant, and its known limits (after Mitchell et al., 2019); write "not for" first, so no one relies on the workflow where it was never tested (§19.7). (2) It was tested only on those inputs and uses; outside them there is no evidence (§19.7).
**19.8** (1) The new build, runs and peer test, with their checks, safeguards, card and defense; reused A11 parts are not graded again unless revised (§19.8, §19.5). (2) A result alone overstates readiness; the limit tells a non-specialist where not to rely on it (§19.7–19.8).

### Faded examples {.unnumbered}
**19.1 Lucía's row.** Analyzing the budget: the business default is a check point, but the guide's override applies, because the board votes on spending from it (the analysis moves money): approval gate. Choosing scholarship recipients: keep with a person (deciding about people).
**19.2 A rated speed.** Compare the summary's 5,300 rpm with the datasheet's 5,000 rpm: verdict contradicted; correct the summary from the datasheet.
**19.3 Survey answers.** Personal data about other people: no under consumer terms; under institutional terms only if the part needs it and the rules allow, and the consent form keeps responses with the course team, so no outside tool without the course team's approval. To pass: ask the instructor and use only an approved tool after removing classmates' names and identifying details, or sort the answers by hand.
**19.4 The tutoring center.** Nearest first after the center's rule: (2) the tutored course's syllabus: AI for explanations only, so no AI-drafted answers to graded work; (3) FERPA: the center's session notes about the students it tutors are education records, so they stay out of AI tools. Accept also: a tutee's own work goes into a tool only with the student's permission and under the center's rule.
**19.5 A lab-report checker.** Typical: a complete report whose calculations are right. Different: a report with masses in milligrams or a different experiment's format. Edge: a report with a milliliter-to-liter slip in one concentration, or a missing raw value; the checker must flag it, not supply a number.
**19.6 Feedback on tutoring notes.** With three runs each, the one-sentence gap is a lead: it cannot show that the workflow treats the names differently, or that it does not. Next: record it as a lead and run a bigger test (at least 10 runs per version, counting rule fixed in advance), or a second name pair.
**19.7 Sam's card.** Tested on: three datasheets (metric; US units; no stall-torque value), tool kind, model if shown, date. Results: right; right after his unit check; produced a value not on the datasheet, caught at his check. Limits: the tool may fill in missing values, so stall torque is read from the datasheet; one tool and model; check point at every value.
**19.8 Lucía's A13 sheet.** Run 2: matching the reversed entry as an ordinary line is wrong against the answer key: verdict contradicted. Run 3 (edge, her choice): for example, a bank fee missing from the ledger, checked against the key. Revision: use "reconcile" for one step only and "match" for the line step, then rerun the input that failed.

- **20.6** (§20.6) A portfolio goes to new readers outside the course, with no contract, and can be forwarded; the data classes decide again, and others' information is not yours to publish.

Before and after as given; **what changed:** corrected (source 3 reclassified from "reliable" to "a press release; lead only"); **why:** the press release overstated the sample; **trail:** checked the study itself (the primary source), verdict on the press release's claim: contradicted (or partly supported), with the study's citation and date; **declaration line:** e.g., "No AI used for this check," or the tool, its purpose and what was rejected.

1. Strong answers take a position and use §20.2: one exact, dated, attributed sentence can show awareness of the field (the WEF's 2025 estimate from employers' 2024 expectations, all trends combined), but such numbers say nothing about the student and are easily misquoted as AI numbers; most portfolios are stronger without one. Weak answers treat the numbers as facts or reject all forecasts.

## Chapter 21 — Your Personal AI Code of Practice {#sec-appendix-e-ch21 .unnumbered}

### Check Yourself {.unnumbered}

- **21.1** (1) A commitment names a moment you would notice and an action you or someone else can trace, with your own evidence as the reason; a slogan has neither moment nor action (§21.1–21.2). (2) Policy and a profession's code bind you whether or not you write them down; your code adds your own commitments inside them (§21.1, §21.3).
- **21.2** (1) It fails "moment" ("when I use AI" is not a moment you would notice as special) and "action" ("careful" leaves no trace); it also has no reason (§21.2). (2) A rule says what you must do, not why the line matters to you; the reason question asks for your own evidence, so a rule counts only together with it (§21.2). (3) Verification, data, disclosure, and one on delegation and oversight, or risk, or fairness (§21.2).
- **21.3** (1) The assignment: the stricter rule wins, and a personal code never loosens a rule (§21.3). (2) The rules you are under (cited, not copied); "where one is stricter, it wins"; the owner you would ask, by role (§21.3).
- **21.4** (1) Tool facts change in months, commitments should last years; a dated note keeps the fact and its date together (§21.4). (2) No: a new kind of input is one of Chapter 12's re-test triggers, which are also review triggers, so it sends you back to your code before the review date (§21.4). (3) Marks show which lines applied and which never came up, so the review can keep, revise or retire lines on evidence; an unread code behaves like a soft gate (§21.4).
- **21.5** (1) A classmate reads your draft aloud, applies the trigger test line by line, checks the boundaries line and names one line to revise; you record that line before and after, with the question it failed and the question it now passes (item 7 of the brief) (§21.5).

### Faded examples {.unnumbered}

- **21.1 Marketing student.** "AI drafting permitted with disclosure" = policy (her course); "Be transparent" = slogan; "Before I post client copy that a tool drafted, I check every product claim against the client's fact sheet" = personal commitment (it needs a reason); "The approved tool's free tier allows 50 messages a day (as of October 2026)" = dated tool note.
- **21.2 Student teacher.** For example: *When an AI tool states a fact about the curriculum that will go into my lesson or feedback, I check it against the curriculum document and note the check, because two of ten AI-stated curriculum facts in my A5 table were wrong.* Test: moment (an AI-stated curriculum fact headed for a lesson) ✓; trace (the noted check) ✓; reason (his own A5 result) ✓.
- **21.3 Finance intern.** (2) For example: *Before I put any client information into an AI tool, I use only the firm's approved tool and note which tool in my work file, because last month I had to report pasting a client's summary into an unapproved one.* (3) The compliance office, which owns the handbook.
- **21.4 Co-op student.** (2) A model update or retirement (the model he tested is being retired) and a change of job or school (the co-op). (3) The line naming the AI tool his lab allows, and its model, becomes a dated note, "as of [month year]."

### Review Questions A {.unnumbered}

1. **(c)** "Before I submit work, I list every AI use in my declaration." (a) is a slogan (M1); (b) is policy; (d) is a dated tool note (M4).
3. **(d)** Fourteen lines are hard to recall, so many will not come to mind when needed (M6). (a) is M6 itself; (b) misstates the rule (5–7 with four required); (c) invents a rule.
5. A trigger in a code tells you that one of your commitments applies now; a re-test trigger (Chapter 12) is an event that should make you test a tool's fit again. In a code, Chapter 12's re-test triggers become review triggers for the whole code.
7. **(d)** It is allowed: a personal code may be stricter, but never looser. (a) and (b) misstate the rule; (c) a personal code binds no one else.
9. **(b)** Tool facts change in months, while commitments should last years. (a) overcorrects M4 (tools may be named, in dated notes); (c) and (d) are invented rules.
11. **(c)** It is a basis for judgment: several principles may apply with different weight. (a) and (d) misread the phrase; (b) the code does contain principles and guidelines.

### Review Questions B {.unnumbered}

1. "Protect patient privacy" — slogan; "The pharmacy's handbook: no patient data in unapproved software" — policy (employer); "Before I ask an AI tool about a drug interaction, I remove anything that identifies a customer, and I check the answer in the pharmacy's reference" — personal commitment (add a "because"); "The pharmacy's chatbot runs model X (as of March 2027)" — dated tool note; "Know and respect existing rules (ACM 2.3)" — professional code; "Be careful" — slogan. Rewrite, for example: *Before I rely on a dose or interaction from an AI tool, I check it in the pharmacy's reference and initial the check, because last month I caught an AI answer with the wrong maximum dose.*
3. Fixed line, for example: *When a draft involves anything from students' records, I use only the office's approved tool and note the tool in the file, because last term my own draft with a student's ID number ended up in a free tool's history.* Boundaries line: *This code works inside my course's AI rules, my institution's data classes and the office's written AI rule; where one is stricter, it wins; when a rule is unclear, I ask the office manager.*

### Review Questions C {.unnumbered}

1. Strong answers take a position and use the ACM code's description of itself (a basis for decision-making, not a procedure) and the trigger test: triggers make commitments usable at the moment of action, while choosing commitments, weighing them and handling cases no trigger names still take judgment. Many conclude that triggers support judgment rather than replace it. Weak answers treat a code as either a pure checklist or pure intuition.
3. Strong answers disagree or qualify: tools, rules and jobs change, so a code needs a review date, review triggers and dated notes (section 21.4; the ACM's 26-year gap); some note that keeping old versions is a useful record of how one's practice changed. Weak answers say a code is "just for the portfolio" or that it must change constantly.

### Spaced Review {.unnumbered}

1. It shows what the AI did and what you did for that entry: tools, purpose, what you accepted, rejected or revised, how you verified it, and where your judgment shaped the work (section 20.3).
3. Any safeguard from A13 written in the "when, I, because" form with the student's own evidence, for example (constructed): *Before my study workflow's flashcards go into my review deck, I check each card against my textbook page, because my A13 peer test found an error.*

### Case Study Questions {.unnumbered}

1. In 1992 many people saw computing work as purely technical and the web was in its infancy; by 2018 computing work could affect people's lives and livelihoods in ways that may not be intended or even predictable.
3. Strong answers set an interval no longer than six months, or tied to the next job or term, justified by how fast the tools in their field change, and turn one ACM principle into a commitment that passes the trigger test, for example (2.5) *When a tool I rely on is updated, I re-run my three test inputs before using it again, because a model update changed my results in a Chapter 12 bake-off.*

### Final Bridge {.unnumbered}

- **FB1. (c)** No evidence: a tool's own "yes" is never a source; check an index or open the work (sections 8.2–8.3). (a) a second question to the same tool is not independent; (b) the tool's naming is not the record; (d) a model is not an expert.
- **FB3. (b)** Little on its own: each way of handling a blank is an assumption, and all can be wrong (section 11.2). (a) agreement among methods is not evidence that they are right; (c) leaving blanks out is itself a choice; (d) overcorrects.
- **FB5. (a)** When it makes errors and the groups' base rates differ, the three cannot all hold (section 16.3). (b) is Chapter 16's M4 (a better choice would fix it); (c) and (d) are unrelated misreadings.
- **FB7.** (a) Treasurer → spreadsheet (ZIP code, birth date, major, payment status) → a free chat tool, under its consumer terms (storage, possible review or reuse depend on the terms) → output list → treasurer. (b) ZIP code, birth date and major are quasi-identifiers: together they can identify a person without a name (section 15.2). (c) For example, likelihood medium and impact medium for members' data kept or reused under the tool's terms; inferred unless the terms were read and quoted. (d) Avoid: do the lookup with a filter in the spreadsheet itself, no AI tool; risk owner: the treasurer (or the club president). Reduce: only a tool that the university's data classes allow, with only the columns needed. (e) No AI output was wrong; the harm is on the input side, so the tree does not apply; the data-flow map and the heat map do.
- **FB9.** Disagree. As of October 2026, the U.S. Copyright Office's position (2025 report) is that U.S. copyright protects what a person authors; output a tool produces from a prompt is not protected, though your own expression, selection, arrangement and changes can be (section 18.3). Writing the prompt does not make you the author of the image; the tool's terms may assign you whatever rights the provider has, which is a different question. Strong answers use human authorship and separate terms from copyright.

### Lab notes {.unnumbered}

- **Lab 21.2.** Expect generated "codes" to be mostly slogans; few or no lines pass all three questions, and none can pass "reason" for the student, because the tool has no access to the student's evidence.
- **Lab 21.3.** Use only the excerpts provided; the 2018 version names machine-learning systems and asks that systems whose future risks cannot be reliably predicted be reassessed often in use (principle 2.5).

## Chapter 23 — Philosophical Debates: Minds, Meaning and Responsibility {#sec-appendix-e-ch23 .unnumbered}

### Check Yourself {.unnumbered}
**23.1** (1) A stated premise is written in the argument; an unstated one is assumed but not written. A map draws an unstated premise with a dashed outline, because it is the reader's reconstruction (inferred) (§23.1). (2) It shows exactly where the two sides part ways, so the disagreement becomes smaller and clearer (§23.1). (3) The strongest fair version of a view, one its holders would accept; without it, a debate is won against a straw man (§23.1).
**23.2** (1) He proposed the imitation game in its place and treated sustained, satisfactory answers in the game as the evidence to use; he did not claim that the machines of his day think (§23.2). (2) (1) A program manipulates symbols by their form (syntax); (2) form alone is not enough for meaning (semantics); (3) the person in the room follows the rules and understands no Chinese. The robot reply accepts premise 2 and adds connections to the world: a program linked to cameras and motors might understand. Searle answered that the camera signals would reach the person as more symbols (§23.2). (3) It raised the share of games in which the models were judged human from 36–38% to 56–73%. The authors describe the test as a measure of how people tell humans from machines; Turing proposed such behavior as the evidence to use, and Searle argued that it cannot settle understanding (§23.2).
**23.3** (1) Phenomenal consciousness is experience, something it is like to be the system; moral status is having interests that matter morally for their own sake. They are linked but distinct (§23.3). (2) A self-report is a claim to check, accepted by both sides; Butlin et al. check a system's design against indicator properties derived from scientific theories (§23.3). (3) Each has a stake in the answer: Suleyman leads Microsoft AI, the AI division of a company that sells AI products; Anthropic sells AI products and acted on its welfare uncertainty (§23.3).
**23.4** (1) The practice rule assigns duties in coursework or a workplace; it does not settle whether blame is always just when no one could foresee what a system would do (§23.4). (2) Premise 1: holding someone responsible requires control and foresight. Premise 2: learning systems act in ways their makers and operators cannot predict. Conclusion: a responsibility gap opens; society must accept it or stop using such systems (§23.4). (3) The person nearest an automated system absorbing blame for a failure they had little control over (Elish, 2019) (§23.4).
**23.5** (1) New, surprising and valuable (Boden, 2004) (§23.5). (2) Neither automatically: "creative" is about the output; authorship asks whose choices shaped it; ownership asks who can explain, defend and stand behind it; legal authorship is a separate question in Ch. 18 (§23.5).
**23.6** (1) Side A: meaningful work is at stake, and whether AI enriches or diminishes it depends on how it is deployed and how tasks are redesigned (Bankins & Formosa, 2023). Side B: less paid work may not be a loss at all (Keynes, 1930/1963; Danaher, 2019) (§23.6). (2) They come from different countries and firms, measure different things (output per hour, earnings and hours, employment), cover different dates, and one is descriptive (§23.6).
**23.7** (1) They are researchers' estimates about the future, not measurements (§23.7). (2) An assessment: a review of evidence developed with more than 100 experts and backed by more than 30 countries and organizations, recording where experts disagree; it does not recommend any policy (§23.7).
**23.8** (1) The question, a map, side A, side B, the hardest objection and reply, what would change your view, an AI Use Declaration; your view appears only in its own labeled paragraph (§23.8). (2) Tools can produce plausible summaries attributed to the right person that the person never wrote; an AI tool's "yes" is never a source (§23.8; Ch. 8).

### Faded examples {.unnumbered}
- **23.1 jobs op-ed:** Reason 2: companies always cut costs when they can. Unstated premise (dashed): writing ad copy is most of what marketing jobs involve (or: if a task can be automated, the job will be cut). Objection: the team's week also includes customer research, campaign planning, client meetings and brand judgment, which denies the unstated premise; or "always" is an overgeneralization, which targets reason 2.
- **23.2 Turing's objection from consciousness:** The objection: a machine must feel what it writes, not only produce words, to think. It targets reason 2 (we grant other people minds on the evidence of their behavior). Turing's reply: by that standard you could never know that another person thinks either; we extend minds to others on the evidence of behavior.
- **23.3 companion robot:** (b) a self-report produced by the system (via its makers): a claim to check, not evidence of enjoyment. (c) a measured result about residents (if the testers are independent): evidence about people's loneliness, not about the robot's mind.
- **23.4 paralegal's clause:** The paralegal: skipped the date check the firm's procedure requires, so some culpability is fair; blamed alone while the provider and the signing lawyer escape, they could become a moral crumple zone (Elish's term). The lawyer: culpability (signed without reading that page) and moral accountability to the client (law: Ch. 18). Fix: an approval gate in which the signing lawyer checks AI-drafted dates against the source (forward-looking responsibility, named owner).
- **23.5 chord progression:** Whose choices: the student's (choosing, changing two chords, writing the melody), plus the tool's suggestions and the patterns it was trained on. Who answers: the student, who can explain, defend and stand behind the song (ownership, Ch. 10).
- **23.6 jobs post:** No: the authors call the result an early, descriptive indicator, not a causal estimate, and the gap shrinks with education controls. Sentence: "In U.S. payroll data through June 2026, employment of 22- to 25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations was 19% below the level it would have reached had it kept pace with peers in less-exposed occupations; the authors call this descriptive, not causal (Brynjolfsson, Chandar & Chen, 2026)."
- **23.7 council member's claim:** Unstated premise (dashed): only superintelligent AI can cause harms worth regulating. Objection: documented present harms in city-like services (bias, opacity, errors; Chapters 11, 16, 17) deny that premise; and ordinary AI use is already regulated in places, for example, as of October 2026, the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (TRAIGA) requires a governmental agency to tell people they are dealing with AI (Ch. 18).
- **23.8 responsibility-gap plan:** Disputed premise: whether responsibility requires control and foresight (Matthias) or our practices can stretch to cover such cases (Tigard). Hardest objection depends on the lean (for a "gap" lean: Tigard's flexibility of practices; for a "no gap" lean: Elish's warning that blame lands on the nearest person). View: in a separately labeled paragraph, with what would change it. Either lean can earn full marks.

### Your Turn keys (where a single answer exists) {.unnumbered}
- **23.2 octopus argument:** Premise 1: meaning links form to something outside language (what a speaker intends, what the words are about). Premise 2: a model trained only on text receives only form. Claim: such a model produces form without meaning. Piantadosi and Hill deny premise 1: meaning can come from the relations among concepts (conceptual role), which a model's internal states could capture.

### Review Questions A {.unnumbered}
1. A premise the argument relies on but does not state; the map draws it with a dashed outline, labeled "inferred," because it is the reader's reconstruction (§23.1).
3. A three-premise reconstruction: (1) A program manipulates symbols by their form (syntax). (2) Form alone is not enough for meaning (semantics). (3) The person in the room follows the rules and understands no Chinese. Conclusion: running the right program is not by itself enough for understanding (§23.2).
5. A system that stitches together sequences of linguistic form it has seen, guided by probabilities of how they combine, without reference to meaning. They did not claim language models are useless; the paper was mainly about the risks of ever-larger models (§23.2; Case Study).
7. Phenomenal consciousness: experience, something it is like to be the system. Moral status: interests that matter morally for their own sake. Separate because a being's interests might matter for reasons other than experience (for example goals of its own), and evidence about one does not settle the other (§23.3).
9. Premise 1: responsibility requires control and foresight. Premise 2: learning systems act in ways their makers and operators cannot predict. Conclusion: a responsibility gap opens; society must accept it or stop using such systems (§23.4).
11. (a) reported (the developer's own claim); (b) forecast (estimates about the future); (c) measured (independent researchers, a method you can read) (§23.6; Ch. 22).

### Review Questions B {.unnumbered}
1. Claim: the tutor understands every student. Stated reason: students say it understands them. Unstated premise (dashed): if students feel understood, the tool understands them. Evidence: on Turing's view, consistent behavior across varied tests is evidence of understanding; on Searle's and Bender's, no behavior settles it (contested, §23.2). Either reading earns credit if the map states both fairly. On either view, measured learning gains would support a narrower claim (it helps), and students' reports alone (public belief, an ELIZA-effect risk) or the tool's own statements (claims to check) would not support the claim as written.
3. Actors: the vendor (built the tool), the hospital (deployed it), the nurse (followed the ranking), the patient. Link: 2, checked before use, could have caught it. Gap: culpability (a busy nurse; on Elish's view, a possible moral crumple zone) and moral accountability (only the vendor can examine why). Forward-looking duty: the hospital names a decision owner and requires a second check for low-priority rankings above a symptom threshold.

### Review Questions C {.unnumbered}
1. Model answer, either side; neither is the correct side, and marks go to the reasoning standard (each side at its strongest, sources, a labeled view). *Agree:* practice rules (ownership, decision owners, gates, Ch. 10–14) apply whatever the answer, so decisions about use do not wait for it. *Disagree:* the answer matters for how far people rely on outputs (the ELIZA effect), for whether understanding-based tasks such as tutoring or counseling are appropriate, and for responsibility (if a system understood, would it share blame?). Strong answers state the other side at its strongest and label the view.

### Spaced Review {.unnumbered}
1. A trigger names a situation and an action ("when X, I do Y") that you can recognize at the moment of use; a slogan states a value with no check (Ch. 21).
3. It splits the text into tokens, scores every possible next token, picks one, adds it and repeats (Ch. 3).
5. Not really: no one can check 200 schedules in ten minutes, so approvals become routine. A real gate gives the approver time, the evidence (conflicts shown first) and the power to say no (Ch. 14).

### Case Study Questions {.unnumbered}
1. Turing did not claim that the machines of his day think; he proposed replacing the question, not answering it, and treated sustained, satisfactory answers as the evidence to use. So, by Turing's own framing, the 2026 result is the kind of evidence he asked for; Searle argues that such evidence cannot settle understanding. Either reading earns credit if both are stated fairly.
3. No AI output was shown to be wrong: the systems did what the study asked; the case is a debate, not a failure.
5. Researchers who do not sell AI products, using a published method (for example indicator assessments by independent consciousness scientists), with their data and reasoning open to checking; ideally reviewed by people on both sides.
